clue.text: Seizes one million quid

blocks.note: the single stroke I is how a crossword writes the number one
M is the standard abbreviation for a million
quid is British slang for pounds sterling, singular and plural alike

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is three money words in a row, which is exactly the wrong picture: the answer is what officialdom does to your property, not a sum you might have in your pocket.
explanation.definitionFit: To impound is to take goods into official custody, so it is seizing carried out under legal authority rather than by force.

clue.text: Policeman's tips for potential overdose

indicators.note: tips are the extreme ends of a thing, so the word asks for the outermost letters and nothing between them

blocks.note: the two ends of the word, first and last
OD is the everyday shorthand for an overdose

explanation.walkthrough: The surface offers a constable's tip-offs about a possible overdose, which reads as one continuous thought and hides the join between the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: PLOD is British slang for a police officer, taken from PC Plod in the Noddy children's books, and like the definition it names one man.

clue.text: Athletic person climbing in tight army gear

indicators.note: a down entry read by climbing runs from the bottom of the grid upwards, so the letters arrive in the opposite order
'in' says the letters are already sitting inside the words that follow rather than being defined by them

blocks.note: six letters run consecutively across the end of one word, all of the next and the start of the third

explanation.walkthrough: "Climbing in" reads as one phrase about squeezing into tight kit, and that is its job on the surface; solving it means hearing two separate instructions in those two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A gym rat is someone who all but lives at the gym, so the definition names the person by the habit rather than by build or sport.

clue.text: Chaucerian character in Canterbury who sang Hallelujah, ultimately

indicators.note: at the very end is what the word means, so each of the four words gives up only its closing letter

blocks.note: the four words in order, each contributing its final letter

explanation.walkthrough: Canterbury and Chaucer push you towards pilgrims, so you look for a person; the letter wanted is a written symbol instead, which is the other sense of character.
explanation.definitionFit: A yogh is a letter of the Middle English alphabet Chaucer wrote in, so "character" here means a written symbol, not somebody in a story.

clue.text: Flush is source of water agitation

blocks.note: a shaft sunk to reach water underground
a to-do is a fuss or commotion

explanation.walkthrough: Sitting next to a source of water, "Flush" wants to be plumbing; it is the money sense, meaning comfortably supplied with cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean having money to spare: flush is the informal "plenty of cash on hand", and the answer is its settled, respectable version.

clue.text: Risk regressive revolution as German leader

indicators.note: something regressive moves backwards, so the word it describes is written in the opposite direction

blocks.note: to take a chance is to take a risk
a revolution is one full roll, turned round here

explanation.walkthrough: "Revolution" is doing double duty on the surface, where it belongs with German history, while the wordplay only wants its plain physical sense of a single turn.
explanation.definitionFit: Germany's head of government holds the title Chancellor, so the definition points at an office by naming the country that uses it.

clue.text: Studied Shakespearean role at National Theatre

blocks.note: the title part of one of the tragedies, a king who divides his kingdom
NT is how the London company signs itself

explanation.walkthrough: "Role" rather than "character" is the tell: the clue wants the name of a part an actor is cast in, and that name then needs a house to be played at.
explanation.definitionFit: To have learnt a subject is to have studied it until you know it; both are past tenses, and this is the British spelling of the word.

clue.text: Dog-sit for Spooner and give too many treats?

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of two neighbouring words as he spoke

blocks.note: a collie is a working dog
to sit for a painter is to model
trade the opening sounds of those two words and say the result aloud

explanation.walkthrough: A Spooner clue defines the answer straight and then describes it with the initial sounds swapped, so the work is done backwards: find the swapped phrase in the clue, then untangle it.
explanation.definitionFit: To mollycoddle is to indulge someone with far more care and comfort than they need, which is what handing out endless treats amounts to.

clue.text: Airship left large current, free to go north then east

indicators.note: north is up the page, so a down entry sent that way is read from the bottom back to the top

blocks.note: L is the standard abbreviation for left
a plain synonym, not the clothing-size L
I is the symbol for electric current in a circuit
to be rid of something is to be free of it
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.walkthrough: "Left" and "large" both look like the one-letter abbreviations L; only one of them is, and the count of squares is what settles which.
explanation.definitionFit: A dirigible is a powered, steerable airship — the word itself means steerable, which is what separates it from a balloon that drifts.

clue.text: Colour of uniform that man adopts

indicators.note: to adopt is to take somebody into the family, so one piece takes the other inside itself

blocks.note: the pronoun a crossword uses for an unnamed male
U is uniform in the radio alphabet

explanation.walkthrough: "Colour of uniform" reads as one phrase and invites you to think of khaki or navy; the uniform is a letter, not a garment.
explanation.definitionFit: Hue is the property that makes one colour differ from another, so it stands as a plain synonym for colour itself.

clue.text: Other ranks visibly embarrassed about group of knights

indicators.note: to come about is to turn right round, the way a boat does, so the piece it touches is written the other way

blocks.note: army shorthand for soldiers below commissioned rank
someone visibly embarrassed goes red, and the colour is turned round

explanation.walkthrough: Other ranks are the soldiers of a British army unit who hold no commission, and OR is the abbreviation the papers lean on constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: An order is a fellowship bound by a shared rule; the Garter and the Bath are orders of knights, so this is definition by category.

clue.text: One often inflexible doctor reversing course to plug new inhaler

indicators.note: to reverse course is to turn back the way you came, so the letters run in the opposite direction
plugging a gap means filling it from the inside, so this piece drops into the middle of the other
made afresh is what new means, and letters made afresh do not keep the arrangement they arrived in

blocks.note: all seven letters of the word, reused in a fresh order
DR is the title before a doctor's name, here written the other way round

explanation.walkthrough: "Doctor" is one of the commonest anagram signals in the business, so it reads as the instruction; here it is the abbreviation, and the small word "new" is doing the shuffling.
explanation.definitionFit: A hardliner holds to a strict position and will not compromise, so the definition names the person by that rigidity rather than by any policy.

clue.text: Electrician finally wiring to ground - disaster narrowly avoided

indicators.note: the word marks the last thing in a sequence, so it takes the closing letter of the word before it

blocks.note: the letter the word ends on
connecting a circuit to the earth for safety

explanation.walkthrough: Earthing is the British term for what an electrician elsewhere calls grounding, which is why the trade surface reads so smoothly and gives nothing away.
explanation.definitionFit: A near thing is an escape by the smallest of margins, and the sense belongs to the whole phrase rather than to either word alone.

clue.text: E-mail edited to speechify better

indicators.note: editing a text means moving its parts about, so the letters come out in a different arrangement

blocks.note: five letters rearranged, the hyphen ignored
to orate is to make a speech, usually a grand one

explanation.walkthrough: "Better" looks like a comparison sitting at the end of a sentence about e-mail; it is a verb, and verbs are what definitions of this answer have to be.
explanation.definitionFit: To ameliorate is to make something better, and "better" is being used here as a verb — to improve — rather than as a comparison.

clue.text: Put out sea-god's declaration exiling setter

indicators.note: to exile somebody is to send them away, so the letter named beside it is banished from the phrase

blocks.note: a sea god announcing who he is says I'M POSEIDON
the person who wrote the clue calls himself I

explanation.walkthrough: The whole spoken sentence is the fodder, which is unusual and easy to miss — you are meant to hear a god introduce himself, then take one letter out of what he said.
explanation.definitionFit: To impose on somebody is to put them out, to inconvenience them by asking too much; a two-word phrasal verb answering a two-word phrasal definition.

clue.text: Manifest completed before time

indicators.note: the word places one piece ahead of the other, so what follows it is written second

blocks.note: when something is over it is completed
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.walkthrough: "Manifest" reads first as the ship's cargo list, a noun; it is the adjective here, meaning plain to see, and the definition has to match that.
explanation.definitionFit: Overt means done openly and in plain sight, and manifest in its adjective sense means obvious to anybody looking — the same idea in a different register.

clue.text: Increasingly rush through half-forgotten speeches at party

indicators.note: half the word has slipped the mind, so only the opening half of its letters is still on the page

blocks.note: the front half of the eight-letter word
the DUP is the Democratic Unionist Party of Northern Ireland

explanation.walkthrough: British crosswords treat the party initials — DUP, SNP, SDP — as ordinary vocabulary, so "party" is very often three letters rather than a celebration.
explanation.definitionFit: To speed up is to go progressively faster, so the setter spells the sense out in two words instead of offering a single synonym.

clue.text: Give an account of Chester river, including top of stony bed

indicators.note: to include something is to take it in, so the outer word closes around what comes next
the top of a word is where it starts, which in a down entry is also its highest letter

blocks.note: the Dee runs through Chester in north-west England
the opening letter of that word
a crib is a baby's bed

explanation.walkthrough: "River bed" is sitting in the clue waiting to be read as one thing, and it never is: the river and the bed are two separate pieces with a letter wedged between them.
explanation.definitionFit: To describe something is to set out in words what it is like, which is exactly what giving an account of it means.

clue.text: Merseyside town, origin of grisly pirate

indicators.note: an origin is where a thing starts, so this points at the opening letter of the word after it

blocks.note: Bootle sits on the Mersey just north of Liverpool
the first letter of that word

explanation.walkthrough: The surface promises a grisly pirate from the north-west coast, which is a picture, not a parse; the definition is the last word on its own and it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To bootleg is to make and sell copies illegally, and to pirate is the verb for the same trade — both are about unlicensed copying.

clue.text: Calm down, perhaps uplifted by signature expression of condolences

indicators.note: something uplifted has been raised, and raising a piece in a down entry makes it read the other way

blocks.note: perhaps signals an example, EG, and here it stands on its head
a tag is the signature a graffiti writer sprays
RIP is carved on gravestones, short for rest in peace

explanation.walkthrough: Three separate scraps of shorthand in a row, and the surface — a signed sympathy card — is smooth enough that none of them looks like an abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Get a grip is the idiom for taking hold of yourself, used exactly where you would tell somebody to stop panicking.

clue.text: Wrong answer written by teacher

blocks.note: A is the standard abbreviation for answer
British schoolchildren address a woman teacher as Miss

explanation.walkthrough: "Wrong answer" is a phrase the eye takes in one gulp, and that is the trap: only the first word is the definition, and the second is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Amiss means out of order or not as it should be — a synonym for wrong that turns up mostly after a verb, as in "something is amiss".

clue.text: Admission in court's beginning to crack criminal cases

indicators.note: a beginning is the first thing there is, so only the opening letter of the word is taken
cracking a safe means getting inside it, so this letter forces its way into the middle of the others
a criminal acts outside the rules, and letters that break the rules abandon the order they were given in

blocks.note: the five letters of the word in a new order
the letter that word opens with

explanation.walkthrough: "Criminal cases" is a real legal phrase and reads as one unit, which is what hides the fact that the adjective is an instruction and the noun is raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: Access is the right or the means of getting in, and admission is the same idea named from the other side of the door.

clue.text: Become suspicious of cryptic master holding everything back

indicators.note: something cryptic is hard to read straight off, and letters out of their usual order are exactly that
to hold a thing is to keep it enclosed, so one piece wraps round the other
in an across entry back means right to left, so the piece runs in the opposite direction

blocks.note: the six letters of the word in a fresh order
everything is ALL, written the other way

explanation.walkthrough: "Cryptic master" reads as a compliment to a setter, which is the setter enjoying himself: the first word is the instruction and the second is the material it works on.
explanation.definitionFit: To smell a rat is to sense that something dishonest is going on — a whole-phrase idiom resting on the rat as a byword for treachery.

clue.text: Swimming pool inspires non-heterosexual desire

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, so the longer word draws the shorter one inside itself

blocks.note: a lido is an open-air public swimming pool
bi is the short form of bisexual

explanation.walkthrough: Lido is a British word you meet far more often in crosswords than at the water's edge, and setters use it whenever they need a four-letter pool.
explanation.definitionFit: Libido is the psychoanalytic name for sexual drive, so desire is the everyday word for the same appetite.

clue.text: Round of game after pawn's lost by Charlie

indicators.note: what is lost has gone missing, so the letter named beside it drops out of the longer word

blocks.note: Charlie is C in the radio alphabet
a partridge is a game bird, shot in season
P is the chess symbol for a pawn, and it is the letter that goes

explanation.walkthrough: "Round of game" sounds like a hand of cards or a shooting party, which is the surface doing its work; game is a bird, and round is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A cartridge is one complete round of ammunition — case, propellant and bullet in a single unit, which is what shooters call a round.

clue.text: Beautiful women not covered in fashion magazine

indicators.note: a cover sits on the outside, so with the covers gone the first and last letters are stripped away

blocks.note: belles are beautiful women, from the French for beautiful

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as a caption about magazine covers, and the word "covered" is doing two jobs at once: picture on the surface, instruction underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: Elle is a long-running international fashion glossy, so the definition names the answer by saying what sort of thing the title is.

clue.text: Lower visibility of marshland traps leader of expeditionary force

indicators.note: to trap a thing is to hold it captive inside, which is what one piece does to the others here
the leader heads the line, so this hands over just the first letter of the word it introduces

blocks.note: a bog is wet, spongy marshland
the opening letter of that word
F is the standard abbreviation for force

explanation.walkthrough: The be- prefix turns a noun into a verb meaning cause to be covered in, the same shape as becalm and bedevil — worth knowing, because setters build words this way often.
explanation.definitionFit: To befog something is to cover it in fog, and fog is precisely what lowers how far anybody can see.

clue.text: Rapid foxtrot by topless performers

indicators.note: topless means missing whatever sits on top, and in a down entry the top is the opening letter

blocks.note: Foxtrot is F in the radio alphabet
the cast is the company of performers in a show

explanation.walkthrough: A dance and a troupe of dancers make a tidy picture, and both halves of it are really shorthand: one letter from the radio alphabet, one word with its head removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Fast and rapid are plain synonyms for moving at speed — not the other sense of fast, which means firmly fixed in place.

clue.text: Drunkard takes Coke product half-heartedly

indicators.note: the heart of the word is a doubled letter, and doing it by halves keeps only one of the pair

blocks.note: coke is a coal-based fuel, and burning it leaves this behind

explanation.walkthrough: Coke next to a drunkard points straight at the drink, and it is the fuel: coal baked until the gas is driven off, which burns dirty.
explanation.definitionFit: A sot is a habitual drunkard, an old word that survives now mainly in crosswords and in older writing.

clue.text: Commonwealth citizen accommodated in urban glade's high-rise

indicators.note: to be accommodated is to be housed inside, so the letters are lodged consecutively within the words that follow

blocks.note: eleven letters run straight on across the three words, apostrophe and hyphen ignored

explanation.walkthrough: Eleven letters is a long span to hide, so a setter has to build a plausible sentence around it; the tower-block picture exists only to carry the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Bangladesh is a member of the Commonwealth, so a Bangladeshi is one instance of the class the definition names.
